categories.name: Access Control
categories.blurb: Limits who and what can reach your systems and CUI, granting only the access each user, process, or device actually needs.

categories.name: Awareness and Training
categories.blurb: Makes sure everyone who touches your systems understands the risks and knows how to perform their security duties.

categories.name: Audit and Accountability
categories.blurb: Records what happens on your systems so activity can be traced to individuals and suspicious behavior can be investigated.

categories.name: Configuration Management
categories.blurb: Keeps systems in a known, hardened state by controlling baselines, settings, and changes over their life cycle.

categories.name: Identification and Authentication
categories.blurb: Make sure every user, process, and device is uniquely identified and proves who it is before touching your systems.

categories.name: Incident Response
categories.blurb: Be ready to detect, handle, report, and practice responding to security incidents before they become disasters.

categories.name: Maintenance
categories.blurb: Keep equipment maintenance controlled so servicing tools, remote sessions, and outside technicians cannot expose your data.

categories.name: Media Protection
categories.blurb: Protect, mark, transport, sanitize, and dispose of the disks, drives, and paper that hold sensitive information.

categories.name: Personnel Security
categories.blurb: Vet people before granting access and lock things down when they leave or change roles.

categories.name: Physical Protection
categories.blurb: Controls that keep people, facilities, and equipment holding sensitive data physically safe from unauthorized access.

categories.name: Risk Assessment
categories.blurb: Practices for finding, rating, and reducing security risks and vulnerabilities across your systems.

categories.name: Security Assessment
categories.blurb: Ongoing review of whether your security controls actually work and staying on top of fixing the gaps.

categories.name: System and Communications Protection
categories.blurb: Safeguards for network boundaries, encryption, and how information moves between and within your systems.

categories.name: System and Information Integrity
categories.blurb: Keeping systems clean and trustworthy by patching flaws, blocking malware, and watching for attacks.

questions.text: Do you limit system access to only authorized users, the processes acting for them, and approved devices?
questions.why: Unrestricted access lets unauthorized people or devices reach CUI and cause harm.
questions.fix: Define an authorized user and device list, then enforce it with account and access controls.

questions.text: Do you limit each user's access to only the transactions and functions their role is permitted to perform?
questions.why: Users with more access than they need expand the damage a compromised account can do.
questions.fix: Map roles to allowed transactions and enforce those permissions in each system.

questions.text: Do you verify and limit connections to and use of external systems you do not control?
questions.why: External systems outside your control may not protect CUI to your standards.
questions.fix: Define terms for external system use and verify them before allowing connections.

questions.text: Do you control what information is posted on publicly accessible systems to keep CUI off them?
questions.why: CUI accidentally published to public systems is exposed to anyone on the internet.
questions.fix: Designate approvers and review content before it is posted to public-facing systems.

questions.text: Do you control how CUI flows within and between systems so it only moves in approved ways?
questions.why: Uncontrolled information flow can push CUI into places or connections that lack protection.
questions.fix: Document approved flow paths and enforce them with firewalls, proxies, or DLP rules.

questions.text: Do you separate duties among different people so no single individual can complete a sensitive task alone?
questions.why: Concentrating conflicting duties in one person makes fraud or misuse harder to detect.
questions.fix: Identify conflicting duties and assign them to separate individuals or roles.

questions.text: Do you apply least privilege, giving users and processes only the access needed to do their work?
questions.why: Excess privileges give attackers and mistakes a wider path to sensitive resources.
questions.fix: Review account privileges and remove any access that is not required for the job.

questions.text: Do you require routine, non-security tasks to run from non-privileged accounts rather than admin accounts?
questions.why: Using privileged accounts for everyday work exposes them to malware and phishing.
questions.fix: Issue separate standard accounts for daily use and reserve admin accounts for admin tasks.

questions.text: Do you stop non-privileged users from running administrative functions and log any such attempts?
questions.why: Unchecked privileged actions by ordinary users can bypass security controls unnoticed.
questions.fix: Restrict admin functions to privileged roles and audit-log attempts to use them.

questions.text: Do you limit repeated failed logon attempts, for example by locking the account after a set number?
questions.why: Unlimited login tries let attackers guess passwords through brute force.
questions.fix: Configure a lockout threshold and delay after a defined number of failed attempts.

questions.text: Do you show users a privacy and security notice consistent with CUI rules before they log in?
questions.why: Without a use notice, users may be unaware of monitoring and handling obligations.
questions.fix: Add an approved system-use banner that displays before authentication completes.

questions.text: Do you lock sessions and hide the screen after a period of inactivity to block onlookers?
questions.why: Unattended, unlocked screens let anyone nearby view or use an active session.
questions.fix: Enable an inactivity timeout that triggers a session lock with a pattern-hiding display.

questions.text: Do you automatically end user sessions when defined conditions, such as inactivity, are met?
questions.why: Sessions left open indefinitely give attackers a lingering foothold to hijack.
questions.fix: Set session termination policies that close sessions after the defined trigger.

questions.text: Do you monitor and control remote access sessions to your systems?
questions.why: Unmonitored remote connections are an easy, unseen entry point for intruders.
questions.fix: Route remote access through managed gateways and log and monitor those sessions.

questions.text: Do you protect remote access sessions using approved cryptography such as a VPN or TLS?
questions.why: Unencrypted remote sessions can be intercepted, exposing credentials and CUI.
questions.fix: Require FIPS-validated encryption (VPN or TLS) for all remote connections.

questions.text: Do you route all remote access through a limited number of managed control points?
questions.why: Scattered remote entry points are hard to monitor and easy to overlook.
questions.fix: Funnel remote traffic through a few managed access points and block direct paths.

questions.text: Do you require explicit authorization before allowing remote execution of privileged commands or access to security data?
questions.why: Remote privileged actions are high value targets that attackers seek to abuse.
questions.fix: Define and approve which privileged commands may run remotely, and deny the rest.

questions.text: Do you authorize wireless access and set its configuration requirements before any device connects?
questions.why: Unauthorized wireless connections give attackers a way in without physical access.
questions.fix: Establish a wireless authorization policy and required settings before enabling access.

questions.text: Do you protect wireless access with authentication and encryption?
questions.why: Open or weakly secured wireless can be joined or eavesdropped by outsiders.
questions.fix: Configure WPA2 or WPA3 Enterprise with strong authentication on all wireless networks.

questions.text: Do you control and authorize the connection of mobile devices to your systems?
questions.why: Unmanaged mobile devices can carry malware in or CUI out unnoticed.
questions.fix: Define a mobile device policy and enforce it with mobile device management (MDM).

questions.text: Do you encrypt CUI stored on mobile devices and mobile computing platforms?
questions.why: A lost or stolen mobile device without encryption exposes any CUI it holds.
questions.fix: Enable full-device or container encryption on all mobile devices that handle CUI.

questions.text: Do you limit or prohibit the use of portable storage devices on external systems?
questions.why: Portable media used on uncontrolled systems can spread malware or leak CUI.
questions.fix: Set a policy that restricts or bans portable storage on external systems and enforce it.

questions.text: Do you restrict system access so that only devices and components owned, provisioned, or issued by your organization can connect?
questions.why: Advanced adversaries pivot in through unmanaged or personal devices that sit outside your security controls.
questions.fix: Enforce device identity and posture checks (for example certificate-based network access) so only organization-issued assets connect.

questions.text: Do you use secure information transfer solutions, such as cross-domain gateways, to control data flows between separate security domains?
questions.why: Without controlled cross-domain transfer, an intruder in one domain can move CUI freely into or out of another.
questions.fix: Deploy a vetted cross-domain or guarded transfer solution that inspects and mediates all flows between domains.

questions.text: Are your managers, administrators, and users made aware of the security risks and policies tied to their work?
questions.why: People unaware of risks and rules are more likely to make choices that expose CUI.
questions.fix: Deliver security awareness training that covers relevant risks, policies, and procedures.

questions.text: Are personnel trained to carry out the security responsibilities assigned to their specific roles?
questions.why: Staff who lack role-specific training cannot reliably perform their security duties.
questions.fix: Define role-based security duties and provide training for each relevant role.

questions.text: Do you train staff to recognize and report potential indicators of insider threat?
questions.why: Insider threats go undetected when staff do not know the warning signs or how to report them.
questions.fix: Add insider threat awareness to training, covering indicators and reporting steps.

questions.text: Do you train staff at hire, after major cyber events, and at least annually to recognize advanced threats and social engineering?
questions.why: APT campaigns often start with tailored phishing and social engineering that untrained staff will not spot.
questions.fix: Add advanced threat and social engineering content to onboarding, annual training, and post-incident refreshers.

questions.text: Do you include hands-on practical exercises, aligned with current threat scenarios and tailored to user roles, in your security awareness training?
questions.why: Passive training does not build the reflexes users need to react correctly under a real APT attack.
questions.fix: Run role-based simulations (for example phishing tests and tabletop drills) with feedback to reinforce correct behavior.

questions.text: Do you create and retain audit logs sufficient to monitor, investigate, and report unauthorized activity?
questions.why: Without adequate logs, unauthorized activity cannot be detected or investigated.
questions.fix: Identify security-relevant events and configure systems to log and retain them.

questions.text: Can you trace logged actions to the specific individual user responsible for them?
questions.why: Actions that cannot be tied to a person prevent accountability for misuse.
questions.fix: Use unique user IDs and capture them in audit records for every tracked action.

questions.text: Do you periodically review and update which events your systems log?
questions.why: Logged events that are never revisited can miss new threats and relevant activity.
questions.fix: Schedule regular reviews of your logged event list and adjust it as needs change.

questions.text: Are the right people alerted when the audit logging process fails?
questions.why: Silent logging failures create blind spots where activity goes unrecorded.
questions.fix: Configure alerts for logging failures such as errors or full storage capacity.

questions.text: Do you correlate audit review, analysis, and reporting to investigate suspicious activity across systems?
questions.why: Reviewing logs in isolation misses attacks that span multiple systems.
questions.fix: Aggregate logs (for example in a SIEM) and correlate them during investigations.

questions.text: Can your audit system reduce records and generate reports for on-demand analysis?
questions.why: Raw, unsummarized logs are hard to analyze quickly when an incident occurs.
questions.fix: Deploy tooling that filters, summarizes, and reports on audit records on demand.

questions.text: Do your systems synchronize clocks to an authoritative source so audit timestamps are accurate?
questions.why: Inconsistent clocks make it impossible to reconstruct the true order of events.
questions.fix: Point all systems at an authoritative time source using NTP.

questions.text: Do you protect audit records and logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion?
questions.why: Attackers who can alter or erase logs can hide their tracks entirely.
questions.fix: Restrict access to logs and tools and store copies in tamper-resistant storage.

questions.text: Is management of audit logging limited to a small set of privileged users?
questions.why: If monitored users can manage the logs, they can disable oversight of their own actions.
questions.fix: Assign audit management to a separate, limited group distinct from general admins.

questions.text: Do you maintain baseline configurations and inventories of your systems throughout their life cycle?
questions.why: Without a known baseline and inventory, you cannot tell what a system should look like or spot drift.
questions.fix: Document hardware, software, and firmware baselines and keep an up-to-date inventory.

questions.text: Do you establish and enforce secure configuration settings for the IT products in your systems?
questions.why: Default or loose settings leave systems with unnecessary weaknesses to exploit.
questions.fix: Adopt hardening benchmarks and enforce them with configuration management tools.

questions.text: Do you track, review, approve or reject, and log changes to your systems?
questions.why: Unmanaged changes can introduce vulnerabilities or outages without a record of who or why.
questions.fix: Run a change management process that reviews, approves, and logs every change.

questions.text: Do you analyze the security impact of changes before you implement them?
questions.why: Changes made without impact analysis can silently weaken security controls.
questions.fix: Require a documented security impact assessment as part of change approval.

questions.text: Do you define, document, and enforce physical and logical access restrictions for system changes?
questions.why: If anyone can make changes, unauthorized or untracked modifications become likely.
questions.fix: Limit who can make changes and enforce those limits with access controls and approvals.

questions.text: Do you apply least functionality by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities?
questions.why: Every extra feature or service adds attack surface that can be exploited.
questions.fix: Disable or remove capabilities that are not required for the system's purpose.

questions.text: Do you restrict or disable nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols, and services?
questions.why: Unused ports and services are common footholds for attackers.
questions.fix: Inventory running services and ports, then disable those that are not needed.

questions.text: Do you control which software can run using an allowlist or blocklist policy?
questions.why: Without software execution controls, unauthorized or malicious programs can run freely.
questions.fix: Deploy application control that permits approved software and blocks the rest.

questions.text: Do you control and monitor software that users install themselves?
questions.why: Unmanaged user-installed software can introduce malware or unvetted vulnerabilities.
questions.fix: Set a user-installed software policy and enforce and monitor it with endpoint controls.

questions.text: Do you maintain an authoritative source and repository that defines the approved, trusted components allowed on your systems?
questions.why: Without a trusted baseline, tampered or malicious components introduced by an adversary look indistinguishable from legitimate ones.
questions.fix: Establish a signed, authoritative repository of approved hardware, firmware, and software with integrity references.

questions.text: Do you use automated mechanisms to detect misconfigured or unauthorized components and correct them?
questions.why: Advanced actors exploit configuration drift and rogue components faster than manual review can catch them.
questions.fix: Deploy continuous configuration monitoring that flags and auto-remediates unauthorized or misconfigured components.

questions.text: Do you use automated tools to continuously discover and inventory the components connected to your systems?
questions.why: You cannot defend assets you do not know exist, and adversaries hide in unmanaged, undiscovered devices.
questions.fix: Turn on automated discovery and inventory tooling that keeps a real-time record of all connected components.

questions.text: Do you uniquely identify every user, process, and device before they connect to your systems?
questions.why: Without unique identifiers you cannot tell who or what took an action, making accountability and auditing impossible.
questions.fix: Issue a distinct account or identifier to each person, service, and device, and stop using shared or generic logins.

questions.text: Do you verify the identity of each user, process, or device (for example with a password or certificate) before granting access?
questions.why: Claiming an identity is not enough; without authentication an imposter can access systems as someone else.
questions.fix: Require every identity to authenticate with a credential such as a password, token, or certificate before access is allowed.

questions.text: Do you require multifactor authentication for privileged accounts and for network access to regular accounts?
questions.why: A single stolen or guessed password can hand an attacker full access, so a second factor sharply reduces account takeover.
questions.fix: Enable MFA (something you have plus something you know) for all admin accounts and remote or network logins.

questions.text: Are your network logins protected by replay-resistant authentication so captured credentials cannot be reused?
questions.why: If an attacker records an authentication exchange, they can replay it to log in unless the mechanism blocks reuse.
questions.fix: Use protocols with nonces, time stamps, or one-time challenges (such as Kerberos or TLS-based auth) for network access.

questions.text: Do you prevent reusing the same account identifier for a defined period after it is retired?
questions.why: Recycling an old username too soon can wrongly tie a new person to a former user's history and access.
questions.fix: Set a policy that retired identifiers are not reassigned until a defined waiting period has passed.

questions.text: Do you disable accounts automatically after a defined period of inactivity?
questions.why: Dormant accounts are easy targets because nobody notices when an attacker uses one that is no longer watched.
questions.fix: Configure systems to automatically disable identifiers that have gone unused past a set threshold.

questions.text: Do you enforce a minimum password complexity and require changed characters when new passwords are created?
questions.why: Weak or trivially altered passwords are quickly cracked or guessed, undermining every other access control.
questions.fix: Set password policy rules for minimum length and complexity and require a meaningful change of characters on reset.

questions.text: Do you block reuse of a password for a set number of previous generations?
questions.why: Letting users cycle back to an old password lets a previously exposed credential become valid again.
questions.fix: Enable password history enforcement so a specified number of prior passwords cannot be reused.

questions.text: Do you require that any temporary password be changed to a permanent one immediately at first logon?
questions.why: Temporary passwords are often predictable or shared, so leaving them in place is a standing risk.
questions.fix: Configure accounts so a temporary credential forces an immediate password change on the first successful login.

questions.text: Do you store and transmit passwords only in cryptographically protected form (hashed or encrypted)?
questions.why: Passwords kept or sent in plaintext can be read outright if a database or network traffic is compromised.
questions.fix: Ensure passwords are salted and hashed at rest and only sent over encrypted channels, never in the clear.

questions.text: Do you obscure authentication feedback, such as masking passwords as they are typed?
questions.why: Displaying credentials on screen lets shoulder surfers or cameras capture them during login.
questions.fix: Configure login prompts to hide password characters and avoid echoing authentication details back to the user.

questions.text: Do you cryptographically authenticate systems and devices in both directions before they are allowed to communicate?
questions.why: One-way trust lets an adversary impersonate a server or device and intercept or inject traffic.
questions.fix: Require mutual (bidirectional) cryptographic authentication, such as mutual TLS or device certificates, between endpoints.

questions.text: Do you block components from connecting unless they are known, authenticated, and confirmed to be in an approved configuration?
questions.why: Untrusted or compromised assets that connect unchecked give adversaries a foothold inside the network.
questions.fix: Enforce network access control that admits only authenticated devices meeting an approved configuration posture.

questions.text: Have you established an incident response capability covering preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery, and user response?
questions.why: Without a defined process, a security event turns into chaos and damage spreads while responders improvise.
questions.fix: Write and adopt an incident response plan with clear phases, roles, and steps, and make sure staff know it.

questions.text: Do you track, document, and report security incidents to the appropriate internal and external authorities?
questions.why: Unreported or undocumented incidents violate contractual obligations and leave leadership and partners blind to threats.
questions.fix: Set up an incident log and reporting workflow that notifies designated officials within required timeframes.

questions.text: Do you periodically test your incident response capability, for example with tabletop or live exercises?
questions.why: A plan that has never been exercised often fails under pressure, revealing gaps only during a real crisis.
questions.fix: Schedule regular tabletop or simulated incident exercises and update the plan based on lessons learned.

questions.text: Do you operate a security operations center capability that monitors your systems 24 hours a day, 7 days a week?
questions.why: APT actors deliberately act during nights and weekends when unmonitored networks give them free dwell time.
questions.fix: Stand up a 24/7 SOC capability, in-house or managed, with on-call staffing for continuous monitoring and triage.

questions.text: Do you maintain a cyber incident response team that can be deployed within 24 hours of an incident?
questions.why: Slow response lets a sophisticated intruder expand access and exfiltrate CUI before containment begins.
questions.fix: Designate and resource an incident response team with a playbook enabling deployment within 24 hours.

questions.text: Do you perform and document maintenance on your organizational systems?
questions.why: Neglected systems accumulate unpatched flaws and failing hardware that attackers and outages can exploit.
questions.fix: Establish a scheduled maintenance program and keep records of the servicing performed on each system.

questions.text: Do you control the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used to carry out system maintenance?
questions.why: Unvetted maintenance tools or people can introduce malware or bypass security while servicing systems.
questions.fix: Approve and inspect maintenance tools and restrict maintenance work to authorized, controlled methods and staff.

questions.text: Do you sanitize equipment of sensitive information before it leaves your facility for off-site maintenance?
questions.why: Devices sent out for repair can carry sensitive data straight into untrusted hands if not first wiped.
questions.fix: Remove or securely erase protected data from equipment before releasing it for external servicing.

questions.text: Do you check diagnostic and test media for malicious code before using it on your systems?
questions.why: Maintenance media can silently carry malware that infects systems the moment it is connected.
questions.fix: Scan all diagnostic and test programs and media for malicious code before introducing them to any system.

questions.text: Do you require multifactor authentication for remote maintenance sessions and terminate them when the work is done?
questions.why: Remote maintenance over external connections is a prime attack path if it lacks strong authentication and clean shutdown.
questions.fix: Enforce MFA on nonlocal maintenance connections and automatically close the session once maintenance completes.

questions.text: Do you supervise maintenance personnel who lack authorized access while they work on your systems?
questions.why: An unescorted technician without clearance could view, copy, or tamper with sensitive data during servicing.
questions.fix: Assign an authorized escort to accompany and monitor any maintenance worker who does not hold the required access.

questions.text: Do you sanitize or destroy media containing sensitive information before disposal or reuse?
questions.why: Discarded or repurposed drives and paper often still hold recoverable data that can leak sensitive information.
questions.fix: Wipe, degauss, or physically destroy media using approved methods before it is thrown out or reassigned.

questions.text: Do you physically control and securely store both paper and digital media that hold sensitive information?
questions.why: Media left unsecured can be stolen or copied, exposing sensitive information without any network intrusion.
questions.fix: Store sensitive paper and digital media in locked cabinets, rooms, or controlled areas with restricted access.

questions.text: Do you limit access to sensitive information on media to only authorized users?
questions.why: If anyone can pick up and read a drive or document, access controls on the network become meaningless.
questions.fix: Restrict who can handle or read sensitive media and enforce it with physical and logical access controls.

questions.text: Do you mark media with the required sensitivity markings and any distribution limitations?
questions.why: Unlabeled media makes it easy for people to mishandle or over-share information they do not realize is sensitive.
questions.fix: Apply clear markings to media indicating its sensitivity level and any handling or distribution restrictions.

questions.text: Do you control and account for media containing sensitive information while it is transported outside controlled areas?
questions.why: Media in transit is easily lost or stolen, and without tracking you may never know it went missing.
questions.fix: Log custody of media during transport and use secured carriers or containers to maintain accountability.

questions.text: Do you encrypt sensitive information on digital media during transport unless it is otherwise physically protected?
questions.why: A lost or intercepted unencrypted drive exposes its full contents, but encryption keeps the data unreadable.
questions.fix: Encrypt sensitive data on portable digital media before it is moved, unless equivalent physical safeguards apply.

questions.text: Do you control the use of removable media, such as USB drives, on your system components?
questions.why: Uncontrolled removable media is a common route for both malware infection and data exfiltration.
questions.fix: Define and enforce a removable media policy, restricting or disabling ports and approving only sanctioned devices.

questions.text: Do you prohibit the use of portable storage devices that have no identifiable owner?
questions.why: Anonymous or found storage devices are a classic attack vector for planting malware inside an organization.
questions.fix: Block use of storage devices with no assigned owner and train staff never to plug in unknown media.

questions.text: Do you protect the confidentiality of backups that contain sensitive information at their storage locations?
questions.why: Backups hold the same sensitive data as production, so an unprotected backup store is an easy target.
questions.fix: Encrypt and access-control backup media and secure the sites, on-site or off-site, where backups are kept.

questions.text: Do you screen individuals before authorizing their access to systems containing sensitive information?
questions.why: Granting access without vetting can place untrustworthy insiders directly next to your most sensitive data.
questions.fix: Conduct background screening appropriate to the role before provisioning access to sensitive systems.

questions.text: Do you protect sensitive systems during and after personnel actions like terminations and transfers?
questions.why: Departing or reassigned staff who keep their old access can retain or abuse entry into sensitive systems.
questions.fix: Disable accounts, recover credentials and assets, and adjust access promptly whenever someone leaves or changes roles.

questions.text: Do you act to protect your systems when adverse information emerges about an individual who has access to CUI?
questions.why: Insider threats and coerced personnel are a favored APT vector for reaching protected information.
questions.fix: Define a process to review and adjust access promptly when adverse personnel information is reported.

questions.text: Do you limit physical access to your facilities, equipment, and computer systems to only the people who are authorized?
questions.why: Unrestricted physical access lets outsiders tamper with, steal, or plug into systems holding sensitive data.
questions.fix: Define who is authorized and put locks, badge readers, or staffed reception at entry points to restricted areas.

questions.text: Do you escort visitors and keep an eye on their activity while they are inside your facility?
questions.why: Unaccompanied visitors can wander into sensitive areas and access or steal information undetected.
questions.fix: Require visitors to sign in, wear a badge, and be escorted by an employee at all times.

questions.text: Do you keep audit logs recording who physically accessed your facilities and when?
questions.why: Without a record of physical entry, you cannot investigate incidents or spot unauthorized access after the fact.
questions.fix: Maintain visitor sign-in sheets or electronic badge logs that capture identity, date, and time of access.

questions.text: Do you control and manage physical access devices such as keys, badges, locks, and access codes?
questions.why: Lost, shared, or unrecovered keys and badges let people enter secured areas without authorization.
questions.fix: Track who holds each key or badge, and collect or deactivate them when someone leaves or changes roles.

questions.text: Do you protect and monitor the physical facility and the supporting infrastructure (power, cabling, HVAC) for your systems?
questions.why: Unguarded facilities and utilities can be sabotaged or exploited to disrupt or access protected systems.
questions.fix: Add physical monitoring (cameras, alarms) and safeguard power, wiring, and environmental controls from tampering.

questions.text: Do you enforce safeguards for protected information when employees work from alternate sites such as home or the road?
questions.why: Remote and home work sites lack office protections, exposing sensitive data to theft or prying eyes.
questions.fix: Set a remote-work policy covering device security, encryption, and physical protection at off-site locations.

questions.text: Do you periodically assess the security risks to your operations, assets, and people from running systems that hold sensitive data?
questions.why: Without regular risk assessments you cannot prioritize defenses against the threats that matter most.
questions.fix: Run a periodic risk assessment that identifies threats, likelihood, and impact to your systems and data.

questions.text: Do you scan your systems and applications for vulnerabilities on a regular schedule and when new threats emerge?
questions.why: Unscanned systems hide known weaknesses that attackers can find and exploit before you do.
questions.fix: Deploy a vulnerability scanner and run it on a set cadence plus whenever significant new flaws are announced.

questions.text: Do you fix the vulnerabilities you find, prioritizing them according to your risk assessments?
questions.why: Finding vulnerabilities does no good if the most dangerous ones are left unpatched and exploitable.
questions.fix: Create a remediation process that ranks findings by risk and tracks fixes to closure within set timeframes.

questions.text: Do you use threat intelligence from open, commercial, or government sources to inform your risk assessments?
questions.why: Risk assessments blind to current adversary tactics miss the threats APT actors are actively using.
questions.fix: Subscribe to and integrate threat intelligence feeds into your recurring risk assessment process.

questions.text: Do you conduct threat hunting to proactively search for indicators of compromise and disrupt intruders?
questions.why: Stealthy APT actors evade automated alerts and can dwell for months until a human hunter finds them.
questions.fix: Establish a recurring threat hunting program that hypothesizes adversary behavior and searches for evidence.

questions.text: Do you use advanced automation and analytics to predict and identify risks to your organization and systems?
questions.why: Manual analysis cannot correlate the volume of signals needed to anticipate advanced, multi-stage attacks.
questions.fix: Adopt analytics tooling (for example UEBA or SIEM correlation) that surfaces predictive risk indicators.

questions.text: Do you document, in your security plan, why each security solution was chosen and the residual risk it leaves?
questions.why: Undocumented rationale hides coverage gaps that a determined adversary can find and exploit.
questions.fix: Record solution selection, rationale, and residual risk determinations in your system security plan.

questions.text: Do you assess how well your security solutions work at least annually and whenever relevant threat information arrives?
questions.why: Controls that were effective yesterday can be bypassed by new adversary techniques if never re-evaluated.
questions.fix: Schedule at least annual effectiveness reviews and trigger reassessment on new threat intelligence.

questions.text: Do you assess, respond to, and monitor supply chain risks for your systems and components?
questions.why: APT actors compromise trusted suppliers to reach many targets at once, as seen in major supply chain attacks.
questions.fix: Evaluate supplier and component risk, and monitor for compromise across your supply chain.

questions.text: Do you maintain a supply chain risk management plan and update it at least annually or after significant threat events?
questions.why: Without a living plan, supply chain defenses go stale as adversaries shift to new upstream targets.
questions.fix: Document a supply chain risk management plan and review it annually and after major threat events.

questions.text: Do you periodically assess your security controls to confirm they are actually working as intended?
questions.why: Controls that are assumed to work but never tested may silently fail and leave data exposed.
questions.fix: Schedule periodic assessments or audits that verify each control operates effectively and document results.

questions.text: Do you create and follow plans of action to correct deficiencies and reduce the vulnerabilities found in your systems?
questions.why: Identified gaps that lack an owner, plan, and deadline tend to linger and never get resolved.
questions.fix: Maintain a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) that assigns owners and target dates to each open deficiency.

questions.text: Do you monitor your security controls on an ongoing basis to make sure they stay effective over time?
questions.why: Controls decay as systems, staff, and threats change, so a one-time check quickly goes stale.
questions.fix: Set up continuous monitoring (automated alerts, periodic reviews) so control drift is caught quickly.

questions.text: Have you developed, documented, and do you periodically update a system security plan describing how you protect your systems?
questions.why: Without a written security plan, protections are inconsistent and impossible to verify or hand off.
questions.fix: Write a system security plan (SSP) covering scope, boundaries, and controls, and review it on a regular cycle.

questions.text: Do you conduct penetration testing at least annually using automated tools and skilled human testers?
questions.why: Only adversarial testing reveals the chained weaknesses an APT actor would combine to break in.
questions.fix: Commission annual penetration tests that pair automated scanning with expert, goal-driven human testing.

questions.text: Do you monitor, control, and protect communications at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of your systems?
questions.why: Unguarded network boundaries let attackers move in and data flow out without being detected or blocked.
questions.fix: Deploy firewalls or gateways at your network perimeter and key internal segments to control traffic.

questions.text: Do you place publicly accessible systems on subnetworks that are physically or logically separated from your internal networks?
questions.why: Public-facing servers on the same network as internal systems give attackers a direct path inward.
questions.fix: Put internet-facing services in a separate DMZ subnet isolated from your internal network by firewall rules.

questions.text: Do you apply secure architecture, development techniques, and engineering principles that build security into your systems?
questions.why: Security bolted on late is weaker and costlier than designing it into systems from the start.
questions.fix: Adopt secure design standards and integrate security reviews into your architecture and development lifecycle.

questions.text: Do you separate regular user functions from system administration and management functions?
questions.why: Mixing admin tools with everyday user access widens the blast radius if a normal account is compromised.
questions.fix: Run management interfaces on separate accounts, systems, or networks isolated from general user activity.

questions.text: Do you prevent unauthorized or unintended transfer of information through shared system resources?
questions.why: Leftover data in shared memory, storage, or caches can leak to the next user or process that reuses it.
questions.fix: Configure systems to clear or isolate shared resources (memory, buffers, temp files) between users and tasks.

questions.text: Do you deny network traffic by default and allow only the connections you have explicitly approved?
questions.why: Allowing everything except known-bad traffic lets novel or overlooked threats slip straight through.
questions.fix: Configure firewalls to deny-all by default and add explicit allow rules only for required, approved traffic.

questions.text: Do you prevent remote devices from connecting to your network and an outside network at the same time (split tunneling)?
questions.why: Split tunneling lets a remote device bridge the internet and your network, bypassing perimeter defenses.
questions.fix: Configure your VPN to route all traffic through the corporate gateway, disabling split tunneling on clients.

questions.text: Do you use encryption or physical protection to safeguard sensitive information while it is being transmitted?
questions.why: Data sent in the clear can be intercepted and read by anyone monitoring the network path.
questions.fix: Enforce TLS, VPNs, or other encryption for sensitive data in transit, or use protected physical channels.

questions.text: Do you automatically terminate network sessions after a period of inactivity or when a communication session ends?
questions.why: Idle open sessions can be hijacked or reused by someone who gains access to an unattended device.
questions.fix: Set session timeouts that drop network connections after inactivity or at the end of each session.

questions.text: Do you establish and manage cryptographic keys for the cryptography used in your systems?
questions.why: Poorly generated, stored, or rotated keys undermine encryption and can expose all the data it protects.
questions.fix: Adopt a key management process covering secure generation, storage, rotation, and destruction of keys.

questions.text: Do you use FIPS-validated cryptography whenever encryption is used to protect sensitive information?
questions.why: Unvalidated or weak encryption may contain flaws that leave protected data readable by attackers.
questions.fix: Configure systems to use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules for protecting sensitive information.

questions.text: Do you block remote activation of collaborative devices like cameras and microphones, and clearly signal when they are in use?
questions.why: Remotely activated cameras or mics can secretly capture conversations and sensitive information.
questions.fix: Disable remote activation of collaborative devices and provide indicators (lights, prompts) when they are on.

questions.text: Do you control and monitor the use of mobile code such as scripts, applets, and macros?
questions.why: Mobile code can run malicious actions on a device the moment a user opens a page or file.
questions.fix: Define a mobile code policy and use controls that restrict or block untrusted scripts, applets, and macros.

questions.text: Do you control and monitor your use of Voice over IP (VoIP) technologies?
questions.why: Unsecured VoIP systems can be eavesdropped on or abused as an entry point into your network.
questions.fix: Set usage rules for VoIP and monitor it, applying authentication and encryption to voice traffic.

questions.text: Do you protect the authenticity of communication sessions so you can trust the other end and detect tampering?
questions.why: Without session authenticity, attackers can impersonate a party or hijack a connection mid-session.
questions.fix: Use authenticated, integrity-protected protocols (like mutual TLS) so both endpoints and messages are verified.

questions.text: Do you protect the confidentiality of sensitive information while it is stored at rest?
questions.why: Stored data left unencrypted can be read directly if a disk, laptop, or backup is lost or stolen.
questions.fix: Enable encryption at rest for sensitive data on servers, endpoints, removable media, and backups.

questions.text: Do you use physical or logical isolation techniques to separate and protect your most critical systems and data?
questions.why: Flat networks let an adversary who breaches one system move laterally to everything else.
questions.fix: Apply physical or logical isolation (for example segmentation or air gaps) around critical assets.

questions.text: Do you identify, report, and correct flaws in your systems in a timely manner?
questions.why: Unpatched system flaws are among the most common ways attackers gain a foothold.
questions.fix: Establish a patch management process that finds, tracks, and applies fixes for flaws promptly.

questions.text: Do you provide protection from malicious code at appropriate points across your systems?
questions.why: Without anti-malware defenses, viruses and other malicious code can spread and compromise your data.
questions.fix: Deploy antivirus or endpoint protection on servers, workstations, and email or web gateways.

questions.text: Do you update your malicious code protection mechanisms whenever new versions or definitions become available?
questions.why: Out-of-date antivirus signatures cannot recognize the newest malware variants circulating in the wild.
questions.fix: Enable automatic updates for antivirus engines and definitions so protection stays current.

questions.text: Do you run periodic scans of your systems and real-time scans of files from outside sources as they are downloaded or opened?
questions.why: Malware can arrive in downloads and attachments and stay hidden until a scan catches it.
questions.fix: Configure antivirus for scheduled full scans plus real-time scanning of files as they enter systems.

questions.text: Do you monitor security alerts and advisories and take action in response to them?
questions.why: Ignoring vendor and threat advisories means you miss warnings about actively exploited weaknesses.
questions.fix: Subscribe to relevant security advisories and assign someone to review and act on them promptly.

questions.text: Do you monitor your systems and network traffic, both inbound and outbound, to detect attacks and signs of potential attacks?
questions.why: Attacks that are not monitored for can progress undetected until serious damage is done.
questions.fix: Deploy intrusion detection or monitoring tools that watch traffic and system activity for attack indicators.

questions.text: Do you identify unauthorized use of your organizational systems?
questions.why: Unauthorized use that goes unnoticed lets intruders or insiders operate freely inside your systems.
questions.fix: Review logs and use monitoring to define normal activity and flag unauthorized or anomalous system use.

questions.text: Do you verify the integrity of security-critical and essential software using root of trust mechanisms?
questions.why: Advanced actors implant tampered firmware or boot code that survives reinstalls and evades normal defenses.
questions.fix: Enable hardware root of trust and verified or measured boot to validate critical software integrity.

questions.text: Do you protect specialized assets (IoT, OT, and government equipment) under enhanced requirements or isolate them on dedicated networks?
questions.why: IoT, OT, and government-furnished devices often lack native security and become an APT entry point.
questions.fix: Bring specialized assets under enhanced controls or segregate them onto dedicated, monitored networks.

questions.text: Do you use threat indicator information from open, commercial, or government sources to guide your intrusion detection?
questions.why: Detection that ignores current indicators of compromise will miss the tools and infrastructure APT actors reuse.
questions.fix: Feed current threat indicators into your intrusion detection and monitoring systems.
